title: Book 2 — Euterpe, Chapter 333
paragraphs: Let us now leave Homer and the “Cyprian” Epic; but this I will say, that I asked the priests whether the tale the Hellenes tell of the events at Ilion is only an idle story, and they answered me thus: they had their knowledge by inquiry from Menelaus himself. After the rape of Helen, they said, a large army of Hellenes came to the Teucrian land to help Menelaus. When the army had come out of the ships to land and had pitched its camp there, they sent messengers to Ilion, and with these went Menelaus himself. When they entered within the wall, they demanded back Helen and the wealth that Alexander had stolen from Menelaus and carried off; and moreover they demanded satisfaction for the wrongs done. The Teucrians told the same tale then and afterwards, both with oath and without oath: namely that in deed and in truth they had neither Helen nor the wealth demanded, but that both were in Egypt; and that they could not justly be compelled to give satisfaction for what Proteus king of Egypt had. The Hellenes, however, thought that they were being mocked, and besieged the city, until at last they took it. When they had taken the wall and did not find Helen, but heard the same tale as before, then they believed the former account, and sent Menelaus himself to Proteus.
